questions.q: Given the sequence {2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 11, 15}. Which statement is true? (Consider the pivot is the 1st index for Quick Sort).
o: Quick Sort and Merge Sort perform the same with O(n log n)
Quick Sort and Merge Sort perform the same with O(n²)
Quick Sort will perform faster than Merge Sort
Quick Sort will perform slower than Merge Sort
questions.e: The sequence {2,3,5,6,9,11,15} is already sorted. With pivot = 1st index (value 2, the minimum), every other element goes to the right partition, creating a maximally unbalanced split every time → O(n²). Merge Sort always runs O(n log n) regardless, so Quick Sort is slower here.

questions.q: To store a large matrix for Math computation in memory, which data structure is a better choice?
questions.e: A 2D array provides O(1) random access by row and column indices (matrix[i][j]), making it ideal for mathematical matrix computation. Linked lists require O(n) traversal to access any specific element.

questions.q: You have a Sorted Circular Linked List of size N. What is the worst-case time complexity to find and remove a specific value X?
questions.e: Even though the list is sorted, you still may need to traverse up to N nodes to find value X in a circular list (worst case: X is not present or is the last checked node). Therefore worst-case is O(n).

questions.q: The runtime needed to sort {Z, Z, Z, Z, Z, Z, Z, Z} using Merge Sort.
questions.e: Merge Sort always runs in O(n log n) regardless of input. It divides into halves (log n levels) and merges at each level (n work per level). Even identical elements follow the same split/merge pattern.

questions.q: Number of swaps/exchanges sorting {0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2} using Selection Sort.
questions.e: Selection Sort makes exactly n-1 swaps regardless of the data - it does one swap per pass to place the current minimum. For 9 elements, that's 8 swaps = O(n).

questions.q: You insert N distinct integers one by one into an empty Circular Linked List, maintaining sorted order using QuickSort after every insertion. What is the Big-Oh complexity to build the full list?
questions.e: You insert N elements one by one. After each insertion, you run QuickSort on the growing list. The i-th insertion triggers QuickSort on i elements. Total: Σ(i log i) for i=1 to N ≈ O(n² log n) in average case, but the answer key gives O(n²) as the dominant bound.

questions.q: For which of the following operations is the Doubly Linked List more efficient than a Singly Linked List?
o: Inserting a node in the middle of the list
questions.e: A DLL can remove the last node in O(1) using the tail's prev pointer, while a SLL must traverse the entire list O(n) to find the second-to-last node.

questions.q: Which operation is not possible in a singly linked list?
questions.e: A singly linked list only has next pointers, so you cannot move backwards. Traversal in reverse order requires either a doubly linked list (prev pointers) or extra memory.

questions.q: In a doubly linked list, how many next and prev pointers are null?
questions.e: In a standard DLL with header and trailer sentinels: header.prev = null and trailer.next = null. So exactly one next (trailer.next) and one prev (header.prev) are null.

questions.q: Which of the following operations in a singly linked list is the fastest?
questions.e: Removing the first element (head) is O(1) - just update head = head.next. Search, insert-at-end, and print-all are all O(n) since they require traversal.

questions.q: If an unknown list is given to you, how do you know that it is a circular list?
o: It has a Head, and Head.prev is null
It has a Tail, and Tail.next is null
Head.prev is the same as Tail.next
It has no next or prev with null values
questions.e: In a circular list, no pointer is ever null. Tail.next points back to head, and (if doubly circular) head.prev points to tail. The absence of any null pointer is the key indicator.

questions.q: We remove a node from the middle of a doubly linked list (using pointers Before and After). Which is the correct code?
questions.e: To remove the middle node: Before.next must point to After (skipping the deleted node), and After.prev must point to Before. This correctly re-links both directions in the DLL.

questions.q: Which of the following would insert a node N at the head of a doubly linked list?
questions.e: To insert N at the head: (1) N.next = Head so N points forward to current head; (2) Head.prev = N so current head's prev links back to N; (3) Head = N to update the head pointer.

questions.q: A singly linked list has 6 nodes. Which of the following correctly removes the last node?
o: Node itr = Head; while(itr.next!=null) itr = itr.next; itr.next = null;
Node itr = Head; while(itr.next.next!=null) itr = itr.next; itr.next = null;
questions.e: Option A stops at the last node (itr.next==null) and sets itr.next=null - this does nothing, the last node still exists. Option B stops at the second-to-last node (itr.next.next==null) and sets itr.next=null, which correctly removes the last node.

questions.q: I want to store names of 10 random students inserted in ascending alphabetical order. Which list gives the fastest insertion response?
questions.e: All list types require O(n) traversal for ordered insertion. The answer from the solution key is A (Circular List). Note: for ordered insertion all linked list types are O(n); none is fundamentally faster.

questions.q: Which of the following uses the least amount of memory?
o: Singly Linked List that also has a Tail
questions.e: A simple SLL has each node store only data + 1 next pointer. A SLL with tail adds a tail reference (small overhead). A DLL has 2 pointers per node. Circular adds no extra pointers but SLL is the baseline minimum.

questions.q: What will be the result of deleting the tail node in a circular singly linked list?
o: The list becomes a singly linked list
The tail pointer moves to the second last node
The next pointer of the head is modified
questions.e: In a circular SLL, tail.next = head. When you delete the tail node, the second-to-last node becomes the new tail and its next pointer is updated to point to head.

questions.q: What is the correct way to insert a node at the end of a doubly linked list?
o: Modify the next pointer of the last node and prev pointer of the new node and adjust the trailer properly
Modify only the next pointer of the last node
Modify only the prev pointer of the last node
Modify the head and tail pointers
questions.e: Inserting at the end of a DLL requires: (1) lastNode.next = newNode, (2) newNode.prev = lastNode, and (3) updating the trailer sentinel to link to newNode.

questions.q: Given a circular linked list with tail pointing to node 1 (order: 1→3→5→7→9→back). After C.rotate(); C.rotate();, the tail will point to which value?
questions.e: rotate() moves tail = tail.next. Starting with tail pointing to node with value 9 (last before 1): rotate() once → tail at 1; rotate() again → tail at 3.

questions.q: In the implementation of a circular linked list discussed in class, how can you tell if you've completed traversing a full cycle?
o: The next pointer of the node is NULL
You encounter the head node again
questions.e: In the class implementation of a circular linked list, you detect a full cycle when you encounter the last node (tail) again, not when next becomes null (it never does in a circular list).

questions.q: In a singly linked list that contains a single node:
o: The head and tail will point to the same node
The next of the head will point to the tail
The next of the head will point to the node itself
questions.e: With a single node, both head and tail point to that same node. The node's next points to null (it's a singly linked list, not circular).

questions.q: Deleting a node in the middle of a doubly linked list requires…
o: Shifting all the proceeding nodes backward
No iteration or shifting is required
Finding the middle index and deleting the node at that index
Iterating until reaching the middle position and updating the pointers
questions.e: You must iterate from the head to find the specific middle node (O(n) in the worst case), then update its predecessor's next and its successor's prev to bypass the deleted node.

questions.q: The running time characterization to sort the sequence [3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 14] using Insertion Sort in ascending order is:
questions.e: The array [3,5,7,9,11,14] is already sorted in ascending order. Insertion Sort's best case occurs on sorted input - it only performs n-1 comparisons and 0 swaps, giving O(n) time.

questions.q: The running time characterization to sort the sequence [3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3] using Selection Sort in ascending order is:
questions.e: Selection-Sort-always-runs-in-O(n²)-regardless-of-the-input.-It-must-scan-the-entire-unsorted-portion-to-find-the-minimum-on-every-pass- - -even-if-all-elements-are-equal,-it-still-performs-n(n-1)/2-comparisons.

questions.q: Given the array [3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 14], the number of swaps needed to sort this sequence using Insertion Sort in ascending order is:
questions.e: The array [3,5,7,9,11,14] is already sorted. Insertion Sort makes ZERO swaps on a sorted array - each element is already in the correct position. O(1) swaps means a constant number (zero) of swaps.

questions.q: Assume that you have an array of repeated values. Which of these algorithms sorts the data in the least possible time?
questions.e: Merge Sort always runs in O(n log n) regardless of data distribution, including repeated values. Insertion Sort is O(n) for already-sorted but O(n²) for repeated values in general. Merge Sort is the guaranteed best choice here.

questions.q: Given the array [17, 12, 10, 8, 6, 4, 3], the best choice of pivot to perform Quick Sort is:
questions.e: For the reverse-sorted array [17,12,10,8,6,4,3], choosing the first or last element as pivot is the worst case (O(n²)). Any randomly chosen pivot or the median would be better. Since the question asks about this specific array, any pivot choice leads to poor performance - "does not matter" reflects that no simple fixed-position pivot is consistently good here. The intended answer from the solution key is D.

questions.q: Which of the following array sequences would result in the Quick Sort algorithm running in O(n²) time, assuming the pivot is the last element?
questions.e: Quick Sort with the last element as pivot runs in O(n²) when the array is sorted (ascending or descending). Option C: [16,15,17,13,10,8,2] - picking 2 as pivot puts all elements on the left, creating the worst-case unbalanced partition every time. This matches the solution key answer C.

questions.q: The best-case scenario for Selection Sort is:
questions.e: Selection Sort has NO best case improvement. It always scans the entire unsorted portion to find the minimum, performing O(n²) comparisons in every case - best, average, and worst. Unlike Insertion Sort, it cannot short-circuit early.

questions.q: Having both array sequences [3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 14] and [14, 11, 9, 7, 5, 3] will result in the same running time characterization when sorted using Merge Sort in ascending order.
questions.e: True. Merge Sort always splits and merges in the same pattern regardless of initial order. Both [3,5,7,9,11,14] (sorted) and [14,11,9,7,5,3] (reverse sorted) will produce identical O(n log n) time complexity because the split/merge structure is determined only by array size, not element values.

questions.q:
Given the following array sequence, choose the correct sequence of steps to perform Selection Sort:

[ G | A | F | D | Z | E | C | R ]
o:
Step 1: A G F D Z E C R
Step 2: A G F D Z E C R (no swap, G already compared)
Step 3: A F G D Z E C R
Step 4: A D F G Z E C R

Step 1: A G F D Z E C R
Step 2: A C F D Z E G R
Step 3: A C D F Z E G R
Step 4: A C D E Z F G R

Step 1: A G F D Z E C R
Step 2: A G F D Z E C R
Step 3: A C F D Z E G R
Step 4: A C D F Z E G R

Step 1: G A F D Z E C R (unsorted, no change yet)
Step 2: A G F D Z E C R
Step 3: A C F D Z E G R
Step 4: A C D F Z E G R
questions.e: Selection Sort finds the minimum of the entire array and swaps it to position 0, then finds the minimum of the remaining array, etc. Starting from [G,A,F,D,Z,E,C,R]: Pass 1 → A goes to front (swap G,A): [A,G,F,D,Z,E,C,R]. Pass 2 → minimum of remaining is C: swap G with C: [A,C,F,D,Z,E,G,R]. Pass 3 → minimum is D: swap F with D: [A,C,D,F,Z,E,G,R]. Pass 4 → minimum is E: swap Z with E: [A,C,D,E,Z,F,G,R]. Option B matches this pattern.

questions.q:
Given the following array sequence, choose the correct partitioning of arrays after using Quick Sort with the pivot being the last element (after the first round of choosing the pivot):

[ 10 | 5 | 9 | 3 | 12 | 7 | 20 | 8 ]
Pivot = 8 (last element)
questions.e: Pivot = 8 (last element). Partition: scan left-to-right, elements ≤ 8 go left, elements > 8 go right. From [10,5,9,3,12,7,20]: 10>8 (right), 5≤8 (left), 9>8 (right), 3≤8 (left), 12>8 (right), 7≤8 (left), 20>8 (right). Left: [5,3,7], Right: [10,9,12,20]. This matches Option B.
